proposal.title: Justice Department Housing Discrimination Case Against Trump Management
proposal.description_short: In 1973, the Justice Department sued Donald Trump, Fred Trump and their company over alleged racial discrimination in rental housing. The 1975 consent decree barred…
proposal.description_medium: The Justice Department sued Donald Trump, Fred Trump and Trump Management in 1973, alleging Fair Housing Act violations. The complaint described Black applicants being denied vacancy information or steered elsewhere. The case ended in a 1975 consent decree barring discrimination and requiring training, equal-housing ads and vacancy lists for the New York Urban League. The decree expressly did not admit liability.
proposal.description_long: The Justice Department filed suit in October 1973 in the Eastern District of New York against Donald Trump, his father Fred Trump, and Trump Management, alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act across 39 buildings containing more than 14,000 apartments. The Civil Rights Litigation Clearinghouse case file says the complaint relied in part on paired testing: white testers were told about vacancies while Black testers were not or were steered to different properties. It also alleged employees used codes beside applicants’ names to indicate race. The defendants counterclaimed for defamation; the court dismissed that counterclaim and allowed the federal case to proceed. The parties resolved the case through a consent decree signed June 10, 1975. It barred discrimination in rental terms and practices, required Donald and Fred Trump to familiarize themselves with the Act, and required advertisements stating that minorities had equal opportunity to apply. Trump Management also had to provide the New York Urban League weekly vacancy lists for two years. The decree expressly stated that it was not an admission of a violation. The record supports the filing, allegations, and negotiated obligations, but not a claim that a court found the defendants liable.

proposal.description_long: The Arms Control Association’s September 1, 2026 analysis of the U.S.–Saudi civil nuclear cooperation agreement says the deal does not require Saudi Arabia to adopt the IAEA Additional Protocol. Instead, it relies on a U.S.–Saudi bilateral safeguards agreement implemented by the IAEA and limited to facilities covered by the nuclear cooperation agreement. The Association says the bilateral arrangement includes some measures beyond Saudi Arabia’s standard comprehensive safeguards agreement, including short-notice inspections at covered sites, but does not provide the broader access to undeclared sites and activities available under the Additional Protocol. The IAEA’s country factsheet independently lists Saudi Arabia’s safeguards agreement under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty as in force since January 13, 2009. The Arms Control Association assesses the narrower bilateral agreement as insufficient to assure the absence of undeclared nuclear activity; that is the organization’s expert assessment, not an IAEA finding that safeguards were bypassed. A precise entry should describe the omission of the Additional Protocol and the criticism of the substitute agreement, while acknowledging the safeguards that remain and attributing the evaluation.

A termination letter cited failure to demonstrate acceptable conduct in Joslin’s role as a biologist and referred to the May incident; Joslin said the action was taken as a private citizen. Narrowing the title to the AP-documented Yosemite case keeps the entry within the evidence. Any broader pattern would require separate agency records and case-specific reporting.

proposal.description_long: On September 18, 2018, the Department of the Interior announced that the Bureau of Land Management had finalized a rule revising the 2016 Waste Prevention Rule, also known as the Venting and Flaring Rule. The regulation covered venting, flaring, and leaks associated with oil and gas production on federal and tribal lands. The Department’s announcement said BLM had found considerable overlap between the 2016 rule and existing state, tribal, and federal regulations. The final rule was published in the Federal Register on September 28, 2018, as “Waste Prevention, Production Subject to Royalties, and Resource Conservation; Rescission or Revision of Certain Requirements.” That primary record identifies revisions to the 2016 regulations and provides the operative provisions. The evidence supports saying that Interior revised key requirements; “rescinded” can overstate the action if it implies that the entire rule was removed. The supplied URL points instead to a Wikipedia page about Facebook and is not evidence for this event. The title and descriptions are therefore corrected to use the official description and date, and the evidence resolution points to the agency announcement and Federal Register text. This draft does not claim environmental consequences beyond what those primary sources establish.
